lead: A shaft that has run for years can break at a stress well below yield. The load repeats, so a tiny crack starts at a notch, grows a little each cycle, and finally the remaining metal snaps. Fatigue design asks one question: at a given stress amplitude, how many cycles will the part survive? The S–N curve answers it, and for steel the endurance limit gives the amplitude below which the part lasts indefinitely. Shafts, axles, springs, bolts and connecting rods are all designed this way, for infinite life or for a stated number of cycles.
prereq: You need: Kf and notch sensitivity from the chapter on stress concentration, and fully reversed bending stress (see Direct, bending and torsional stresses).

blocks.text: Fatigue is failure under a stress that repeats. For a cycle between σ<sub>max</sub> and σ<sub>min</sub> the stress amplitude is σ<sub>a</sub> = (σ<sub>max</sub> − σ<sub>min</sub>)/2 and the mean stress is σ<sub>m</sub> = (σ<sub>max</sub> + σ<sub>min</sub>)/2. Fully reversed loading has σ<sub>m</sub> = 0, so σ<sub>a</sub> = σ<sub>max</sub>. A part whose peak stress is below yield can still fail after enough cycles, in three stages.

Stage 1, crack initiation. Cyclic slip in surface grains forms persistent slip bands with tiny intrusions and extrusions. A notch, scratch or corrosion pit raises the local stress to Kt σnom, so the crack starts there; the notched part's fatigue strength is lower by the factor Kf (see stress concentration).

Stage 2, crack growth. The crack runs across the section, normal to the largest tensile stress, a little on every cycle. Under a microscope the face shows striations, one per cycle. Beach marks are larger curved lines, visible to the eye, where the load changed or the crack paused.
Stage 3, final fracture. The uncracked area becomes too small and breaks in one cycle, leaving a rough, fibrous zone beside the smooth, beach-marked fatigue zone.

sections.h3: The S–N curve and the endurance limit

blocks.text: The R. R. Moore rotating-beam test measures fatigue. A polished round specimen is turned under a constant bending moment, so every surface point sees a fully reversed sinusoidal stress. The machine counts the cycles N until fracture; the test is repeated at several amplitudes S.

Plotted on log–log axes, steel results lie close to a straight line from about (10³, 0.9S<sub>ut</sub>) to (10⁶, S<sub>e</sub>), where S<sub>e</sub> is the endurance limit. Below 10³ cycles is low-cycle fatigue, designed as a static case; from 10³ to 10⁶ is finite (high-cycle) life. The line is S = A N<sup>b</sup>, with b negative:
b = (1/3) log₁₀(Se/0.9Sut) log₁₀ Sf = log₁₀(0.9Sut) + b(log₁₀ N − 3)

S<sub>f</sub> is the fatigue strength (the amplitude that gives a life of N cycles) in MPa; b is the slope per decade of N. Turned round, the life at an amplitude σ<sub>a</sub> is log₁₀ N = 3 + log₁₀(σ<sub>a</sub>/0.9S<sub>ut</sub>)/b.

Ferrous metals show a knee at about 10⁶ cycles (some books use 10⁷); below S<sub>e</sub> they survive indefinitely. Aluminium, copper and most non-ferrous metals have no knee, so they are designed with a fatigue strength at a stated life, never with an endurance limit.

sections.h3: From the test bar to the real part

blocks.text: Se′ is the endurance limit of the small polished test bar. For steels Se′ ≈ 0.5S<sub>ut</sub> up to S<sub>ut</sub> ≈ 1400 MPa, and about 700 MPa above that. The real part is rougher, larger and differently loaded, so Marin's factors reduce it: S<sub>e</sub> = k<sub>a</sub> k<sub>b</sub> k<sub>c</sub> k<sub>d</sub> k<sub>e</sub> Se′.

blocks.text: Shot peening and surface rolling leave the surface in compression, which a crack must overcome, so they raise fatigue strength; corrosion pits and decarburised skins lower it. Some data books add a sixth factor 1/K<sub>f</sub>; then do not multiply the stress by K<sub>f</sub> again.

A part that sees several stress levels uses up its life in pieces. Miner's rule says each block of n<sub>i</sub> cycles at a level whose life is N<sub>i</sub> uses the fraction n<sub>i</sub>/N<sub>i</sub>, and the part fails when the fractions add up to 1:
n<sub>i</sub> is the number of cycles applied at stress level i, and N<sub>i</sub> the life at that level from the S–N line. Levels below S<sub>e</sub> do no damage.
Mean stress (a cycle that does not swing equally about zero) needs the Soderberg, Goodman or Gerber lines in the chapter on fluctuating stresses.

figure.caption: The S–N line falls from 540 MPa at 10³ cycles to 230 MPa at 10⁶ cycles and then stays flat at the endurance limit. The short level line marks Se = 230 MPa from 10⁶ to 10⁷ cycles.

spec.aria: An S–N line falling from 540 MPa at a thousand cycles to 230 MPa at a million cycles and then staying flat as the endurance limit; a short level line marks the endurance limit from a million to ten million cycles.

examples.question: A machined steel shaft has S<sub>ut</sub> = 600 MPa. Take k<sub>a</sub> = 0.85, k<sub>b</sub> = 0.90 and k<sub>c</sub> = k<sub>d</sub> = k<sub>e</sub> = 1.00. The shaft carries a fully reversed bending stress amplitude of 300 MPa. Find (a) Se′, (b) S<sub>e</sub>, (c) the fatigue life.
steps: S<sub>ut</sub> = 600 MPa is below 1400 MPa, so Se′ = 0.5 × 600 = 300 MPa.
examples.answer: Se′ = 300 MPa, S<sub>e</sub> = 230 MPa, and at 300 MPa the shaft lasts about 1.16 × 10⁵ cycles (116 000). At 230 MPa or less it would last indefinitely.

examples.question: The shaft of the first example runs 40 000 cycles at 300 MPa and then 150 000 cycles at 260 MPa. Find the life at 260 MPa, the damage used by Miner's rule, and how many more cycles at 260 MPa it can take.
steps: Life at 300 MPa (first example): N<sub>1</sub> = 1.164 × 10⁵ cycles.
Total so far: 0.344 + 0.405 = 0.748, below 1, so the shaft has not failed.
examples.answer: N<sub>2</sub> = 3.71 × 10⁵ cycles; 74.8 % of the life is used, and about 93 400 more cycles at 260 MPa remain.

import math
b=math.log10(230/540)/3
N=lambda S:10**(3+math.log10(S/540)/b)
D=40000/N(300)+150000/N(260)
print(round(N(300)),round(N(260)),round(D,3),round((1-D)*N(260)))

traps: Using Se′ = 0.5S<sub>ut</sub> as the design endurance limit. It belongs to the polished test bar; multiply by the Marin factors for the real part.
Using an endurance limit for aluminium. Non-ferrous metals have no knee; use the fatigue strength at the required life.
Mixing logarithms. b is the slope of log₁₀ S against log₁₀ N; use log₁₀ in every step, never ln in one step and log₁₀ in the next.
Calling beach marks striations. Beach marks are visible to the eye and mark load changes; striations need a microscope and mark single cycles.
Counting damage from levels below S<sub>e</sub>. In Miner's rule a level at or below the endurance limit adds nothing.

quiz.q: In the R. R. Moore rotating-beam test, what are the mean stress and the stress amplitude?
quiz.a: The mean stress is zero; the amplitude equals the bending stress at the surface. The loading is fully reversed.

quiz.q: Define endurance limit and fatigue strength.
quiz.a: Endurance limit S<sub>e</sub>: the fully reversed amplitude below which a steel survives indefinitely (taken at 10⁶ cycles). Fatigue strength S<sub>f</sub>: the amplitude that gives a stated finite life N.

quiz.q: Why does a sharp notch cut fatigue life far more than it cuts static strength?
quiz.a: Under a steady load a ductile metal yields at the notch and spreads the peak. Under repeated load the peak K<sub>t</sub> σ<sub>nom</sub> cycles every turn and starts a crack there, so the fatigue strength falls by K<sub>f</sub>.

quiz.q: A steel has S<sub>ut</sub> = 700 MPa, k<sub>a</sub> = 0.80, k<sub>b</sub> = 0.85 and k<sub>c</sub> = k<sub>d</sub> = k<sub>e</sub> = 1.00. Find Se′ and S<sub>e</sub>.
For the S–N line of the first worked example, find the fatigue strength for a life of 10⁵ cycles.
Shot peening raises fatigue strength but barely changes tensile strength. Explain.
quiz.a: Peening leaves the surface layer in residual compression, which a crack must overcome before it opens; the bulk, which sets tensile strength, is unchanged.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real load histories are cut into cycles by rainflow counting before Miner's rule is applied. Fracture mechanics follows a crack once it exists with the Paris law, da/dN = C(ΔK)<sup>m</sup>, which sets inspection intervals for aircraft and rail wheels. Very-high-cycle tests past 10⁹ cycles show that even some steels keep failing slowly from inside the part. Search for 'rainflow counting', 'Paris law' and 'very high cycle fatigue'.
